comments.text: The internet wiped out a lot of entry-level jobs. Employers realized they could cast such a wide net that they could afford to wait for the “perfect” candidate - someone already trained with the exact experience they need. Twenty years ago, if you checked 6 out of 10 boxes, you were often considered good enough because you were close, capable, and ready to learn on the job. Now, on-the-job training is virtually extinct. Why pay to train someone new when you can search the internet for someone who already knows how to do the job? Even some general demolition and yard work jobs that can literally be trained in a week still required 3-5 years specific experience. That's what wiped out entry level jobs, now Ai is wiping out / seriously harming mid-level jobs.

I work in a distribution warehouse -- unboxing recreational outdoor products and then boxing them back up to ship.  We pay $20/hr, anyone without a felony record and with a pulse gets a job offer, and we cannot get even close to filling our positions.  Nobody wants to work, the people on staff show up when it's convenient for them, people quit all the time for awful reasons, etc.

I think the salaried job market is completely broken -- phantom job listings, etc.  The hourly job market has plenty of opportunities for people willing to work -- it may not be your preferred job and it might not be a long-term career, but there are decent jobs out there.  From what I've seen, people just prioritize all manner of personal convenience and flexibility over financial stability ... and then complain that they don't have money.  I see this every single day.
